summary:
Chicago was a major film production and distribution center in the early 1900s, before Hollywood became the industry’s leading hub. Essanay Studios, founded in 1907 by George K. Spoor and Broncho Billy Anderson, produced films and employed actors including Charlie Chaplin and Gloria Swanson. Chicago’s film exchanges and nickelodeons helped make it a leading market for film distribution.

In 1909, the Motion Picture Patents Company restricted filmmaking and equipment use to licensed firms. Independent companies formed in response, and many moved west to avoid patent disputes and take advantage of better filming conditions. Chicago’s production industry declined, though the city remained an important exhibition center.

Film production revived in Chicago in the 1980s, with movies including *The Blues Brothers* and *The Breakfast Club*. An Illinois tax credit introduced in 2009 offered filmmakers a 30% break on production costs. In 2011, Cinespace Chicago Film Studios opened on a former steel complex, providing sound stages and production facilities for films and television series.
